Learning Objectives
Understand the epidemiology, anatomy, biomechanics, and mechanism of injury of the
posterior cruciate ligament.
Identify key features of the evaluation of posterior cruciate ligament injuries, including physical
examination maneuvers and imaging study findings.
Assess indications for surgical management and techniques for reconstruction of the posterior
cruciate ligament.
Discuss potential complications, rehabilitation, and outcomes associated with posterior
cruciate ligament injury.

Overview
The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation in
the intact knee.
5% to 20% of all ligamentous injuries to the knee involve the PCL.

Overview
Many PCL injuries go undetected in the acutely injured knee, largely because 50% of
patients with a knee dislocation may present with spontaneous reduction. In addition,
PCL injuries may be isolated or occur in combination with other capsuloligamentous,
meniscal, or chondral injuries in the knee. Although a combined PCL and other knee
injury may be obvious in a knee subjected to high-energy trauma, an isolated PCL injury
may be less obvious because instability often is subtle and patients may be
asymptomatic.1
Epidemiology
The incidence of isolated PCL injuries is undefined in recent studies; however, they are less
common than anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears.

Epidemiology
Emergency department studies report that 37% to 44% of knees subjected to trauma
involve a PCL injury, with additional ligamentous injury present in as many as 95% of
patents with a high-energy injury.2
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:46 PM
AAOS | Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004078
2/28

The PCL consists of a larger anterolateral bundle and a smaller posteromedial bundle3
(Resources 1 and 2).
The PCL has a broader femoral attachment than the ACL, with better healing potential, and the
bony insertion sites of the PCL are three times larger than its midsubstance.4

Osteology
The femoral footprint of the PCL extends more than 20 mm from anterior to posterior.
The anterolateral bundle is more vertical than the posteromedial bundle and inserts on
the anterior roof of the intercondylar notch.2 The trochlear point, in which the cartilage
abruptly turns medially, has been described and may be a reference for tunnel
placement. The center of the anterolateral bundle femoral tunnel should be placed
based on the trochlear point, the medial arch point, and the medial bifurcate
prominence, with the distal edge bordering the articular cartilage.5 The posteromedial
bundle is more oblique than the anterolateral bundle, inserting posteriorly on the lateral
wall of the medial femoral condyle. The anterior margin of the PCL is 2 mm from the
articular cartilage, and the bundle centers are a mean of 12 mm apart.2
The tibial insertion of the PCL is narrower than the femoral insertion and is in the
posterior intercondylar fossa of the proximal tibia. The PCL footprint extends anteriorly
and proximally from the medial meniscus root and the edge of the lateral plateau
articular cartilage to a point 1 to 1.5 cm below the joint line and distal to the posterior
osseous ridge of the tibial plateau. According to reported arthroscopic measurements,
the center of the PCL tibial footprint is 7.8 mm to the shiny white fiber point of the
posteromedial meniscus, 7.4 mm to the champagne glass drop-off of the posterior tibia,
and 5.0 mm horizontal to the medial groove.5 The mammillary bodies lie on either side
of the tibial PCL attachment,6 serving as a tactile and visual cue for identification of the
tibial footprint. The most posterior distal fibers consist of the thicker posteromedial
bundle, and they blend with the periosteum and the posterior capsule to insert distal to
the osseous ridge, cradling the anterior proximal fibers of the anterolateral bundle2
(Figures 1 and 2).

Vascular Anatomy
The PCL is primarily supplied by the middle genicular artery.3
Nerves
Branches of the tibial nerve innervate the PCL.3
Joints and Ligaments
The PCL is associated with the meniscofemoral ligaments of Humphrey (anterior) and Wrisberg
(posterior).2

Joints and Ligaments
The PCL and meniscofemoral ligaments cover almost all the medial aspect of the
intercondylar notch anterior to the medial intercondylar ridge.
Musculature
The stability of the knee depends on the core and hip musculature and the quadriceps and
hamstrings.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The most common cause of PCL injury is a direct blow to the proximal aspect of the tibia.


Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
In athletes, the mechanism of PCL injury usually is a fall onto the flexed knee with the
foot plantarflexed, which places a posterior force on the tibia and subsequently causes
rupture of the PCL. In high-energy trauma, such as motor vehicle collisions (eg,
dashboard injuries), the PCL often is injured in combination with other
capsuloligamentous structures.
Damage to two or more ligamentous structures is considered a multiligamentous knee
injury, and the physician should view this injury as a dislocated knee. The vascular status
of the injured limb and maintenance of reduction should always be carefully assessed in
these patients.
The natural history of PCL injuries is not entirely clear; however, evidence shows that
some of these injuries (especially if combined with other injuries) will progress to
instability, pain, and osteoarthritis of the knee, primarily osteoarthritis of the
patellofemoral and medial tibiofemoral compartments.
Risk Factors
Risk factors for PCL injury include high-energy trauma, participation in soccer or football, and
other contact injuries.
Associated Injuries
Associated injuries include knee dislocation, periarticular fracture, impaction injuries or rim
fractures with resultant bone marrow edema, neurovascular injury, capsulotendinous
avulsions, and ligamentous injuries.
Injury Classification
PCL injuries may occur in isolation or in combination with other injuries.

in Table 1.

Mechanics of Fractures
Tibial and femoral avulsion fractures may occur and may be amenable to immediate repair.7
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
The history of a PCL injury helps to differentiate high-energy trauma from low-energy trauma.
SEND FEEDBACK


Patient History
Concurrent injuries, such as knee dislocation, neurovascular damage, or ligamentous or
skeletal injuries, may further aid in the evaluation.
Physical Examination
The physical examination is specific for a PCL injury, which typically is classified according to
the degree of damage.

Physical Examination
At 90° of knee flexion, a 1-cm anterior offset normally exists between the tibial plateau
and the femoral condyle. In a grade I injury, this step-off is less than 1 cm, but the tibial
plateau is anterior to the femoral condyle. In a grade II injury, the tibial plateau is flush
with the femoral condyle. In a grade III injury, the tibial plateau is posterior to the
femoral condyle.
The posterior drawer is the primary dynamic test used to diagnose a PCL injury, which is
then classified according to the degree of increased posterior tibial translation compared
with the uninvolved knee in 90° of flexion: grade I injury, 3 to 5 mm; grade II injury, 6 to
10 mm; and grade III injury, greater than 10 mm. In partial tears, the degree of posterior
tibial translation may decrease with internal tibial rotation. The quadriceps active test
result is positive if the tibia translates anteriorly between 60° and 90° of flexion in
neutral rotation with resisted knee extension. A combined PCL and capsuloligamentous
injury (ie, PCL injury in combination with damage to other structures, such as the ACL,
posterolateral corner [PLC], or medial side) is indicated by more than 10 to 12 mm of
posterior translation with the knee at 90°.1 The Slocum test, which can be used to assess
for anteromedial rotatory instability, is performed by externally rotating the tibia and
performing an anterior drawer test with the knee flexed to 90°.8 The posterolateral
drawer test is performed by providing a posterior-directed force at the knee with the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:46 PM
AAOS | Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004078
8/28

tibia externally rotated approximately 15° to assess for translation.9 Critical tools for
differentiating isolated injuries from combined injuries are the Lachman test for ACL
injury, varus and valgus laxity testing at 0° and 30°, and the determination of differences
in external and internal tibial rotation.1
Neurovascular Examination
Neurovascular injury must be ruled out by assessing motor and sensory functions and the
dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses.

Neurovascular Examination
In multiligament injuries that result from higher-energy trauma, vascular injuries also
may occur. Multiligament disruption (more than two ligaments disrupted) should
increase suspicion for a knee dislocation. PCL injuries particularly are associated with a
posterior dislocation, 44% of which involve popliteal artery transection.10 If a PLC injury
results from a varus stress, then peroneal nerve injuries also may occur and can be
detected by loss of ankle dorsiflexion and eversion and sensory loss in the first web
space and the lateral aspect of the leg and foot.
Krych et al11 reported that 18 patients of 27 (69%) with a peroneal nerve injury who
underwent multiligament knee reconstruction regained antigravity ankle dorsiflexion
after treatment, which included the use of an ankle-foot orthosis, neurolysis, and tendon
and/or nerve transfer. Among these patients, 38% had a complete nerve palsy, defined
as flaccid ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension and complete sensory loss, and 83%
had a partial nerve palsy, defined as some tibialis anterior or extensor hallucis longus
strength and/or peroneal sensation.11
A thorough neurovascular examination is important in evaluating patients with a PLC
injury because limb-threatening deficits, from a vascular or functional standpoint with
neurologic changes may become apparent. Identification and documentation of
neurologic injury also provides baseline knowledge, particularly if patients are scheduled

9/3/26, 5:46 PM
AAOS | Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004078
9/28

to undergo surgical treatment. Side-to-side differences in pulse examination, which are
common in patients with concomitant injuries, including knee dislocation, warrant
additional workup for vascular injury. Some surgeons advocate obtaining the ankle-
brachial index regardless of normal, symmetric pulses after reduction because of the
short time during which collateral flow can still provide a normal pulse. The ankle-
brachial index is calculated by dividing the systolic blood pressure at the ankle by that at
the brachial artery. A normal result is 0.9, and a lower ankle-brachial index should
prompt additional workup, including CT angiography to further evaluate for vascular
injury.12
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Plain orthogonal radiographs are important initially to rule out fractures and avulsions.

Imaging Studies
The key in the evaluation of radiographs is to recognize that, with the knee (ie, with
intact ACL and PCL) centered in the sagittal plane—a position referred to as the tibial
station—the tibia is anterior to the femoral condyles. To help identify posterior knee
laxity, kneeling stress radiographs also can be obtained. Zero to 7 mm of side-to-side
difference in posterior displacement is consistent with a partial PCL tear, and 8 to 11 mm
of side-to-side difference in posterior displacement is consistent with an isolated,
complete PCL tear. The presence of grade III instability, or more than12 mm of side-to-
side difference in posterior displacement, on kneeling stress radiographs indicates a
combined PCL and PLC (or posteromedial corner) injury.13
Computed Tomography
CT is useful in the evaluation of periarticular fracture patterns.


Computed Tomography
In revision settings, CT provides insight into the degree of bone loss and tunnel
widening.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI has a very high sensitivity and specificity with regard to the diagnosis of PCL injuries.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI complements the patient history and physical examination by depicting the
continuity of the PCL, which helps determine the site and degree of injury (Figure 3). MRI
also may reveal other meniscal, chondral, or ligamentous injuries that may influence
treatment strategies.

ligament injury. B, Follow-up MRI shows healing of the posterior cruciate ligament.

injuries of the knee, in AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1268-1289.)
Differential Diagnosis
Identification of osteochondral injuries that may occur in combination with other ligamentous
injuries (including ACL injuries) is critical to properly manage each injury and ensuring the best
patient outcome.

Differential Diagnosis
Meniscofemoral ligament or meniscal injuries may mimic PCL ruptures.1
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications

Indications
Nonsurgical treatment is reserved for isolated, partial PCL injuries with less than 10 mm
of increased posterior tibial translation; isolated, complete PCL injuries without
symptomatic instability; and patients with low functional demands. Nonsurgical
treatment also is warranted in patients who are unable or unwilling to follow the
prescribed postoperative rehabilitation regimen.
Contraindications
Gross instability in patients with multiligamentous injuries
Persistent instability with functional effects after a trial of nonsurgical management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:46 PM
AAOS | Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004078
12/28

Displaced avulsion fractures with resultant instability
Symptomatic, chronic grade III lesion
Techniques/Procedures
In certain patients, the PCL may heal or generate a provisional bridging scar with nonsurgical
treatment.

Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management consists of bracing with progressive flexion for 4 to 6 weeks. A
dynamic, spring-loaded brace that provides an anterior force has been successful in
appropriate patients because it maintains tibial station and avoids posterior tibial
sag.13,14 Rehabilitation should emphasize isolated quadriceps strengthening and
quadriceps-hamstring isometric co-contractions. In most patients, isolated hamstring
contraction (especially in a flexed position) should be avoided unless in the prone
position.13
Nonsurgical Fracture Fixation
Nondisplaced fractures, particularly in skeletally immature patients, may be amenable to
nonsurgical management; however, close follow-up is warranted to monitor for displacement.
Outcomes
Return to sports activity may be considered as early as 2 to 4 weeks after a PCL injury.

Outcomes
Two outcome studies of nonsurgically managed isolated, grade I or grade II PCL injuries
reported good subjective and objective outcomes, with no functional deterioration and
97% quadriceps and 93% hamstring strength.15,16 In another study of Tegner activity
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:46 PM
AAOS | Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004078
13/28

scores and Lysholm-II Knee Scale scores at 7-year follow-up, 92% of patients with a grade
I or grade II PCL injuries had a good to excellent result after nonsurgical treatment.2
Surgical Management
Indications
Indications for surgical management vary in acute versus chronic PCL injuries.

Indications
Refractory, acute grade II PCL injuries and symptomatically unstable, isolated or
combined, acute grade III PCL injuries are indications for surgical management. For
patients with persistent instability symptoms (particularly when ascending and
descending stairs and inclines) and for combined PCL/capsuloligamentous injuries,
surgical treatment should be considered.
Contraindications
Contraindications to surgical management include substantial comorbidities, inability to
tolerate the procedure, or unwillingness to complete the postoperative rehabilitation program.

Contraindications
Advanced osteoarthritis is a relative contraindication to the surgical management of a
PCL injury. Patients with osteoarthritis may have substantial pain, swelling, and limited
motion postoperatively despite a stable knee. Therefore, they may not experience a
satisfactory outcome.1
Preoperative Planning

14/28

Preoperative imaging studies may be helpful if additional pathology,, including meniscal,
ligamentous, or osteochondral damage, requires surgical management.

Preoperative Planning
If PCL injuries require surgical management, open physes must be assessed to
determine the best approach for graft and tunnel placement. A preoperative discussion
of graft options with the patient is important, with risks and advantages tailored to his or
her level of activity and general health, both of which may affect the condition of an
autograft.
Patient Positioning
A routine examination under anesthesia should be performed.
A thigh tourniquet may be applied to improve visualization.
The patient should be placed in the supine position, and a leg post or a leg holder is used.

Patient Positioning
With the use of a leg post and a flexed foot off the surgical table, the patient should be
positioned close to the edge of the surgical table on the side of the post; the post should
be moved to a position that creates a valgus stress. With the use of a leg holder, the
nonsurgical leg should be padded or placed in a well-leg holder, and the surgical table
should be lowered so the injured leg can flex freely to 90°. Alternatively, the surgical
table may be left flat, and a foot bolster may be placed to allow the knee to rest in 70° to
90° of flexion.
Surgical Approaches
Standard diagnostic arthroscopy is initially performed through a high anterolateral portal with
direct visualization and establishment of the low anteromedial portal. A posteromedial portal
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:46 PM
AAOS | Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004078
15/28

also can be used, particularly if determining placement of the tibial tunnel.
An open posteromedial approach, or safety incision, is performed between the medial head of
the gastrocnemius and the semimembranosus tendon via selected transtibial and tibial inlay
techniques.13
Surgical Procedures
The PCL may be repaired (avulsions), augmented, or independently reconstructed.

Surgical Procedures
Various techniques have been described for the management of PCL injuries, including
the traditional transtibial technique and the open posteromedial approach with an open
tibial inlay, arthroscopic tibial inlay, and an all-inside approach. Single-bundle and
double-bundle graft techniques have been used. A double-bundle graft most closely
reproduces the anatomy of the native PCL by reconstructing the anterolateral and
posteromedial bundles and may provide more continuous stability throughout knee
range of motion with more normal knee kinematics. Single-bundle techniques typically
reconstruct the anterolateral bundle alone.1,13 The anterolateral bundle is secured at
90° with the use of an anterior drawer, and the posteromedial bundle is secured in full
extension.13
To avoid injury, the surgeon must be mindful of the medial meniscus root attachment
given its proximity to the tibial footprint.13 The transtibial technique requires the graft to
course sharply to the femoral tunnel at the so-called killer turn, which may lead to graft
attenuation with cyclic loading.4
Open and arthroscopic tibial inlay techniques can be used to create a blind socket at the
tibial insertion of the PCL. The inlay technique avoids the killer curve that may cause
graft abrasion and increase failure risk because it exits the tibial tunnel and takes a 90°
turn toward the femoral tunnel (Figures 4 and 5).1,13

An all-inside technique with an arthroscopic approach has been described and involves
the use of a quadrupled tibialis anterior or peroneus longus allograft with suspensory
fixation of the tibia and femur. Advantages of all-inside reconstruction include avoidance
of the killer turn during graft passage (attrition to the graft with repetitive
motion/abrasion may still occur), maintenance of the anteromedial tibial cortex, and a
dual-tension construct. This technique may necessitate a long graft (27 to 36 mm) and,
therefore, the use of an allograft (tibialis anterior, peroneus longus) rather than an
autograft (quadriceps).17
Fanelli and Edson18 described an accessory, extracapsular, posteromedial safety incision
that may be used to protect neurovascular structures and confirm accurate tibial tunnel
placement. Alternatively, fluoroscopy may be used during tibial drilling to avoid
neurovascular injury of the popliteal structures.

Graft choices include autografts (central one-third bone-patellar tendon-bone, hamstring
and quadriceps tendon-bone) and allografts (bone-patellar tendon-bone, Achilles tendon
with or without a bone block, and tibialis anterior tendon). No clinical studies clearly
support one technique or graft over another1 (Video 1 ).

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Avulsion of the PCL usually occurs at the femoral attachment and can be repaired with the use
of suture anchors or femoral bone tunnels.

Surgical Fracture Fixation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:46 PM
AAOS | Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004078
19/28

Open reduction and screw-and-washer fixation can be used for large osseous avulsion
fragments from the tibial insertion.2
Postoperative Management
Postoperatively, patients may follow a protocol of progressive weight bearing, prevention of
tibial subluxation posteriorly, and early quadriceps strengthening.13 This conflicts with the
protocol proposed by Fanelli,19 which involves slow, conservative postoperative rehabilitation,
consisting of non-weight bearing for 6 weeks postoperatively and the use of a brace locked in
full extension for 3 to 6 weeks postoperatively, with range of motion and weight bearing
progressing slowly.

Postoperative Management
Concurrent meniscal or articular cartilage procedures may affect weight-bearing status.
In these patients, a postoperative brace is provided. This brace is locked in full extension
the first 4 weeks postoperatively and opened after good quadriceps control is achieved.
Patient risk factors for deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis also should be assessed.1
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
A thorough assessment for additional pathology should be performed because failure to
recognize and manage such pathology concomitant to management of a PCL injury may
jeopardize the success of PCL reconstruction.

Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
All modifiable risk factors, from range of motion goals to comorbidities, should be
optimized.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004078

Complications
Nonunion
Nonunion may occur on rare occasions in patients with a fracture, particularly in active
smokers or patients with risk factors for poor healing and severe instability.
Malunion
Follow-up is critical and should include nonsurgical management to monitor patients for
displacement and intervention as appropriate.
Pain
In patients with chronic PCL deficiency, patellofemoral pain and/or arthritis of the medial
compartment may result from increased posterior translation and dynamic stabilization by the
quadriceps.
Infection
Although deep infection is infrequent after PCL reconstruction, it may occur.

Infection
Irrigation and débridement and possible hardware and graft removal are necessary to
eradicate a postoperative infection. Involvement of infectious disease specialists is
beneficial, and patients generally require 6 weeks of intravenous antibiotic therapy.
Malalignment
Chronic PCL disruption in combination with chondral damage or other ligamentous injury may
exacerbate malalignment issues.
Fracture
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:46 PM
AAOS | Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004078
21/28

Cortical blowout may occur if tunnels are drilled, particularly with nonanatomic placement or
errant tibial- or femoral-sided reaming.
Hardware Failure
Revision may be warranted in patients with hardware failure.
Hardware Malpositioning
Painful hardware may lead to anterior knee pain and, ultimately, the need for hardware
removal after healing; this is more common in patients in whom staples and/or a post/washer
were used.
Insufficiency and Graft Re-tear
Instability may be related to graft malpositioning or additional ligamentous injury that was not
recognized and managed.
No clinical studies clearly support one technique or graft over another; however, tunnel
malpositioning and poor technique may increase stresses through the graft, predisposing it to
rerupture.
Soft-Tissue Reaction
Infrequently, an aseptic soft-tissue reaction may be observed in patients after allograft
reconstruction, leading to synovitis from a host-mediated immune reaction.20 This reaction
should be considered in patients with recurrent effusions after infection and other potential
causes have been ruled out.
Effusion
A postoperative effusion is expected to resorb with time; however, persistent effusion may
indicate potential problems, such as infection, arthrofibrosis, or reinjury.
Stiffness
Knee stiffness generally is uncommon and usually can be resolved via physical therapy. Knee
stiffness is more common after multiligament reconstruction; in some patients, revision

surgery or manipulation under anesthesia may be required.
Hematoma
Hematoma may occur postoperatively and should be monitored closely if it fails to resolve,
particularly with the use of strong/long-term anticoagulants.
Compartment Syndrome
Another possible complication is compartment syndrome, which may result from hematoma
accumulation, neurovascular injury, or fluid extravasation from arthroscopy.21 Compartment
syndrome is an orthopaedic emergency and must be managed vi fasciotomies to preserve
viable structures.
Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
Thromboembolic disease is uncommon; however, patients with a history of deep vein
thrombosis, females who use oral contraceptives, and individuals with a family history of
hypercoagulability, among others, may require anticoagulation therapy.
Neurovascular Injury/Nerve Palsy
Neurovascular injury is a devastating complication of PLC reconstruction, resulting from injury
to the popliteal neurovascular structures during tibial tunnel drilling, penetration of the
guidewire, advancement of the guidewire during tibial tunnel reaming, or direct
contact/winding up of the drill bit with the neurovascular bundle. To prevent such injuries, a
spade tip guidewire is recommended over a trocar tip guidewire in combination with an
oscillating drill and a tapered drill bit rather than a square-shaped drill bit.21 The use of a
posterior soft-tissue retractor with direct visualization through a posteromedial portal also
may be beneficial.
Other Complications
Failure to reference the tibia in relation to the femur may result in misdiagnosis, usually
because of a false-positive anterior drawer test.

Other Complications
Referencing the tibia in relation to the femur is particularly important in patients who
have undergone bypass grafting for vascular injuries, especially in those with a knee
dislocation because of the potential proximity of the graft to tunnel placement.
Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation should focus on quadriceps strengthening.
In general, rehabilitation is slower after PCL reconstruction than after ACL reconstruction,
especially with respect to advancing knee flexion.

Rehabilitation
Isolated hamstring strengthening should be avoided for 12 weeks after PCL
reconstruction. Return to sports activity usually is possible 6 to 9 months
postoperatively.
Outcomes
Biomechanical studies comparing double-bundle and single-bundle PCL reconstruction
techniques reported that double-bundle reconstruction is preferable for decreasing posterior
tibial translation and improving rotational control.22-26 Although this outcome may be
preferred in high-demand athletes, biomechanical advantages were not associated with
superior clinical outcomes. Conversely, isolated, single-bundle reconstruction yielded good
long-term results without functional differences.2
Pearls and Pitfalls
Knee instability occurs less frequently with isolated PCL injuries than with ACL injuries.
